title: FileInspector
excerpt: A cross-platform command-line utility (with an optional GUI) that lists files in a directory tree along with their metadata, exporting to JSON, XML, or CSV.
features: Cross-platform CLI — identical behavior on macOS, Windows, and Linux
Multi-format output — JSON, XML, and CSV from the same scan
Rich metadata capture — beyond name/size/dates: EXIF (photos), ID3 (audio), document properties (author, page count), and other format-specific fields
Filtering — by file name/extension, timestamp range, directory depth, file size, and file attributes
Optional GUI — builds and runs the same command the CLI accepts, for point-and-click scans
Scriptable — designed to slot into cron jobs, CI pipelines, and existing automation without a UI
Diff/compare mode — compare two scans of the same directory to see what changed
advantages: Cross-platform, where the tool it's loosely based on (FileList) is Windows-only
One tool, three output formats — no separate exporters needed per downstream system
CLI-first design means it automates cleanly; the GUI is additive, not required
Single scanning engine behind both CLI and GUI keeps results identical and halves the maintenance burden
Rich metadata capture turns a plain file listing into a genuinely useful catalog (media libraries, document archives)
Diff/compare mode turns it into a lightweight backup/change-audit tool, not just a one-shot lister
pitfalls: Extracting format-specific metadata (EXIF, ID3, document properties) means bundling or depending on multiple parsing libraries — scope creep risk if every format is chased
Very large directory trees (millions of files) need a streaming/incremental writer, not an in-memory scan, to avoid memory blowup
Cross-platform file-attribute differences (Windows attributes vs POSIX permissions) need a normalized schema so output isn't OS-specific
XML output is rarely anyone's first choice today — worth confirming real demand before investing equal effort in all three formats
GUI must stay strictly a thin wrapper around the CLI, or the two will drift and results will stop matching

Filtering engine (name/extension/timestamp/depth/size/attributes)

excerpt: A free service: point it at a property listing and say "analyse this deal" — it fetches the property and its comparables, models it as a short-term rental, long-term rental, renovate-and-resell flip or contractual-position assignment, and returns a personalizable PDF report, emailable to whoever needs to see it.
features: One-instruction flow: give it a listing URL, get back a complete analysed deal
Automatic comparable-listing search — the deal is judged against what else the same money buys nearby
Comp statistics as a distribution: median price/m², spread, and the subject's percentile rank
Market assumptions derived from the comp set rather than guessed, each shown with its sample and editable
Price-drop and days-on-market signals from snapshot history as an absorption proxy
Four strategies modelled side by side: short-term rental, long-term rental, buy-renovate-resell, contractual-position assignment
One shared engine for acquisition costs, taxes, mortgage amortization and holding horizon, so scenarios are actually comparable
Full metric set per strategy: net yield, cash-on-cash, IRR, NPV, payback, equity multiple, break-even point
Pessimistic / base / optimistic ranges with a sensitivity tornado ranking the assumptions that matter
Optional Monte Carlo pass reporting the probability of clearing a target return
Auto-fill from a listing URL, or full manual entry
Editable market defaults per location (nightly rates, occupancy, rent per m², renovation cost per m²)
PDF report with charts, cash-flow waterfalls, amortization tables and a plain-language verdict
Delivery by direct download or email on completion
Per-jurisdiction tax and licensing rules kept in configuration, not in code
Conditional verdict: whether the deal is worth it, under which strategy, and at what threshold it stops being worth it
Free with no paywalled tier or gated sections — a donation button on the finished report, unlocking nothing
Personalizable reports: sender name and logo, editable cover note, section selection, currency and language
Deliver as a PDF download, an emailed report to a third party, or a shareable link to the live version
Verified senders, recipient caps and one-click recipient blocking on all outbound mail
Every analysis stored and re-openable by link, re-runnable against fresh comparables
Internal admin tool to browse, search and filter stored analyses and read aggregate market and cost metrics
Optional account purely for finding past reports, never required to run one
Same verdict regardless of who runs it — no agent mode or buyer mode
Omitted report sections are named as omitted, and the shareable link always resolves to the full analysis
Negotiation-ready output: percentile rank against comparables, local price-cut evidence, and the price at which the deal stops working
stages: Core financial engine: cash-flow model, mortgage amortization, IRR/NPV/payback
The four strategy models on top of the shared engine
Input layer: manual entry plus listing-URL auto-fill and seeded market defaults
Comparable-set retrieval and scoring, with the statistics that describe the local market
Derivation of model assumptions from comps, with per-assumption provenance and override
Scenario ranges, sensitivity analysis and the Monte Carlo pass
Chart generation and PDF report composition
Email delivery and saved/shareable report history
Per-jurisdiction tax configuration packs
Report persistence layer with durable per-report links
Report personalization and branding options
Email delivery with sender verification, rate limits and abuse controls
Internal admin and analytics tool over the stored analyses
Donation integration, privacy policy, retention and deletion tooling
advantages: One instruction replaces an afternoon of manual comparison across listing tabs and a spreadsheet
Assumptions are evidenced by local comparables instead of invented, which is what makes the verdict credible
Answers the comparison question directly — most calculators model one strategy in isolation
Covers contractual-position assignment, which almost no existing tool handles
Ranges and sensitivity make the risk visible instead of hiding it behind one number
A PDF with its assumptions printed is something a partner, accountant or lender can review
Pairs naturally with a scraper: evaluate a whole scraped market, not one apartment at a time
Every input has a defensible default, so a rough answer takes a price and a postcode
Free and account-free removes every reason not to try it, which is how a niche tool gets its first users
Personalized, forwardable reports turn each user into a distribution channel — agents send them to clients
Stored analyses compound into a dataset of what people are really evaluating, which no user could assemble alone
Donations keep it independent, with no obligation to degrade the free path to sell an upgrade
Two natural audiences on opposite sides of the table: agents advising clients, buyers negotiating with brokers
Gives an agent a genuine advisory artifact instead of listing photos, and a buyer evidence instead of an opinion
pitfalls: Garbage in, confident garbage out — a polished PDF lends false authority to bad assumptions
Comparables are asking prices, not transaction prices — they run systematically optimistic and the report must say so
Thin or heterogeneous comp sets in small markets can't support a verdict; the tool has to decline rather than guess
Comparability is a judgement call — renovation state, floor, view, elevator and noise rarely survive into structured fields
Tax rules are jurisdiction-specific, change often, and are the easiest thing to get quietly wrong
Short-term-rental licensing regimes are tightening in many cities and can invalidate a strategy outright
Reliable local market data (real occupancy, achieved rents, renovation costs) is hard to source
Risk of being read as financial advice — needs clear framing and visible assumptions
Renovation cost estimation is genuinely difficult and is where flip models break down
PDF generation with charts is fiddly, and deliverability for emailed reports needs real setup
A free service with real marginal costs — scraping bandwidth, residential proxies, PDF rendering, email — funded by donations that rarely cover them
Anonymous third-party email sending is a spam vector and a fast route to a blacklisted domain if unguarded
Abuse and bot traffic are expensive here in a way they are not for a static site; rate limiting is a launch requirement, not a later refinement
Storing addresses, emails and personal financial assumptions brings GDPR duties — consent, retention, deletion, breach exposure
Branded reports sent by agents invite liability questions about whose analysis the recipient is relying on
Pressure to add an agent-friendly mode that flatters a listing, which would destroy the credibility both audiences depend on
